Hello, this is Frank DeFreitas, and welcome to another week of Holotalk for the week of February 1st, 1999. We have a very interesting guest this week, John Clare, who packs his holography equipment up and takes it down into caves to make holograms of the formations. John just made his first laser pointer hologram, so he's happy he doesn't have to tie the heavy power pack around his leg to crawl for over an hour to get where he's going inside the cave. Just pop the pointer in his pocket, and he's good to go. Now, we have quite a few updates this week on the laser pointer front, but I'm going to save the details for next week's show. Reports are coming in from others. There are many researchers now making holograms using a laser pointer, and it's very encouraging. One person from Norway had his helium-neon laser quit on him over the holidays, and now he's not going to replace it. Steve Michael should have a new report by next week, and I'll be here to tell you about my own experiment using solar power to run my laser pointer, eliminating the needs for batteries entirely. You can see that I've got a lot of people who are using my laser pointer. You can read my first report on this on the laser pointer page. Now, I just got my 10-milliwatt, 640-nanometer laser pointer module, actually a laser diode module, in the mail this week, this past week. So this upcoming week on Holotalk, I'll be running some testing to see how things work out, and I'll report on this as well on next week's show. Now, my guest, John Clare, contacted me last week. He said, I'm going to do a laser pointer on this. At the end of the year, just as Steve and I began to put up information on making holograms with laser pointers, he was very interested in this because he has to lug his helium-neon laser, along with a very heavy motorcycle battery, down into the caves with him. He ties the motorcycle battery to his leg as he crawls through the tight crevices that leads to the larger cathedral underground rooms. He says, I'm going to do a laser pointer on this. For John, being able to make holograms using a laser pointer is a dream come true. He just needs to pop the pointer in his pocket, and off he goes. Now, he just made his first successful laser pointer hologram this week, and he's looking to head into the caves to try it out down there very soon. I had a lot of fun talking with John, and I think he's doing something that's very unique with holography, and I hope you enjoy the interview. Now, I won't be coming back on after the interview is over, so I'll say thank you for tuning in, and hope that you tune in every week for a new Holotalk show. This is Frankie Freitas for Holotalk. Located just off the northeast extension of the Pennsylvania Turnpike and Interstate 78, the studio is a quick, non-stop drive from the New York, Philadelphia, and Baltimore, Washington, D.C. areas. For more information, call the studio's toll-free hotline at... 1-800-458-3525 and begin your own journey with holography today. That's 1-800-458-3525 for more information on attending a Frankie Freitas' holography workshop today. Hello, Frank. John, how are you? All right. Sorry I went home earlier. Oh, that's perfectly okay. No, it was about four years. Is it okay, 10 o'clock now? It's not too late for you, is it? Yes, it's about 10 o'clock. Yes, it's just a little bit after 10. But if I remember right, with the email that you sent me the other night, you were like painting a hologram black at four in the morning, weren't you? Yeah, I don't know what day that was. Was that Sunday night or Monday night or whatever? I remember doing that. Oh, I know those times. I'll tell you what. Doesn't that paint can, when you shake it with the marble in it, sound like ten times as loud in the middle of the night? Yeah. Yeah, almost. I was thinking I'm going to wake the whole neighborhood up, because I usually go outside and spray it. And I'm standing outside shaking this paint can, and you can hear it throughout the whole neighborhood. Yeah, it's all clear park. So we're talking with John, is it Claire? Uh-huh. Okay, John Claire. I just wanted to make sure that I got the last name pronounced, because we've been back and forth with email.

So we're talking with John, is it Claire? Uh-huh. Okay, John Claire. I just wanted to make sure that I got the last name pronounced because we've been back and forth with email, but we really haven't talked to one another until just now. And John does something that I think is so unique that I've never heard about it before. Yeah. Did you have like a 5-milliliter back then or something? Oh, no. I think it was a 2 or 3-milliliter. Yeah. Yeah. The old-fashioned ones that had the epoxy seals on them. Yeah. Yeah. It was at least a 200-foot long thing. Right. But that's good because that keeps people out. Yeah. You have to be pretty dedicated to go through that much trouble to get back in there. That would really turn out really well. Still it is thrilling just to do it and even get a crude image.
